items.title: Phil Flanigan interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998
items.q: we went over to catch Jimmy. And we sat down and then he finished his set and he came over and he goes, “Hey, what are all you guys doing in town?”

ctx.x: Yeah, Coltrane really like, well he predominated the scene much as Parker did I guess.

Even more so, because when Parker was alive they didn’t have all the schools that cranked out a cookie cutterized viewpoint having to do with what’s important in a various categorized box of music. Generally to academia they pick it apart and analyze it. If you do that, something with the most detail, it’s going to be the most interesting, so something like Coltrane is the most interesting. I love Coltrane myself, except for the final period, and that’s good for what it’s good for. But most people, like this kind…

festival that we’re at now, is more traditional, and I can understand why that is. Because like language, jazz has a vocabulary and the vocabulary that’s being spoken in a traditional situation like this is the vocabulary that is the basic words of the language. Now you can get very off on a tangent and get into all sorts of technical terms and that’s what Coltrane would be doing, you know, taking the basic knowledge and taking it off and extrapolating it way out on one tangent or another, and saying, like…
